name: Ancient Louisiana
summary: From about 1700 BCE hunter-gatherers raised the mounds, ridges and plaza of Poverty Point, which UNESCO describes as a residential and ceremonial place, and later Marksville, Troyville and Caddo peoples built burial and platform mounds. No melody or song survives from these centuries. What archaeologists can point to is indirect: feasting pits beside mounds, pebble clusters in burials that were probably rattles, and a Caddo pipe carved as a frog holding a rattle.

name: Native nations
summary: Louisiana is the homeland of nations including the Caddo along the Red River, the Chitimacha of the Atchafalaya Basin and the Houma on the Mississippi, whose song and dance traditions are far older than any written record. European accounts begin only in passing in these two centuries, so almost everything known comes from the nations' own oral histories and from later descriptions of dances, drums and ceremonies.

name: Colonial Louisiana and Congo Square
summary: French and then Spanish rule brings church, school and theater music to New Orleans, from a parish musician hired in 1725 to the city's first known opera in 1796. Enslaved Africans, given Sundays free of work under the 1724 Code Noir, gather to drum, sing and dance wherever they can. Acadian exiles arrive from 1764 and 1765, carrying the songs and fiddle tunes that will grow into Cajun music.

name: Nineteenth century
summary: After the Louisiana Purchase, New Orleans supports a resident opera company in nearly every season while an 1817 ordinance confines the Sunday dances of enslaved people to Congo Square, where they continue into the 1850s. Spirituals and ring shouts take hold in Protestant north Louisiana and the Delta, and French Creole songs from Louisiana reach print in 1867. After Emancipation, Black brass bands and the first Mardi Gras Indian gangs take to the New Orleans streets.

name: Birth of jazz
summary: In New Orleans, Buddy Bolden forms his band in 1895 and brass bands, ragtime, blues and church music fuse into jazz, which travels out by riverboat and touring show and is first recorded in 1917. Blues spreads as mail-order guitars become common, and Lead Belly plays Shreveport as a teenager. On the southwest prairies, Cajun music and Creole la-la house dances take their familiar shape.

name: Recording era
summary: Radio and records carry Louisiana's local styles outward. Shreveport's KWKH launches Jimmie Davis in 1928, the same year the first Cajun records appear, and Creole accordionist Amede Ardoin records between 1929 and 1934. Folklorists John and Alan Lomax record Lead Belly at Angola in 1933 and Black Creole jure singers near Jennings in 1934, while a revival of older New Orleans jazz begins at the end of the 1930s.

name: Postwar boom
summary: New Orleans rhythm and blues pours out of Cosimo Matassa's J&M studio from 1947, and Shreveport's Louisiana Hayride broadcasts country and early rock and roll from 1948 to 1960. In the southwest, zydeco emerges in the late 1940s and swamp pop around 1955, while Baton Rouge bluesmen record swamp blues in Crowley. Cajun music wins a national audience at the 1964 Newport Folk Festival, and the Meters form in 1967.

name: Modern
summary: The first New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival in 1970 opens an era of revival: Mardi Gras Indians record in 1971, a 1974 tribute concert renews pride in Cajun music, and the Dirty Dozen spark a brass band renaissance in the 1980s. New Orleans rap arrives in the late 1980s, bounce in 1991, and Baton Rouge builds its own hip-hop scene. Tribal nations revive and teach their own songs, dances and languages.
